transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Park (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Horizon Head of ML), Priya Shah (Eng Mgr), Raj Patel (CTO)

Summary (auto): cost/unit economics, reserved capacity, caching, next steps to share pricing and benchmark plan

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we got about 40 minutes, should be good to run through your workload and cost questions.
[00:22] Liam O'Connor: Yeah thanks, Maya. Quick context, we're building a user-facing summarization + QA feature, so it's generation heavy. Expecting somewhere in the ballpark of 80-150M tokens a month once live, need to understand unit cost and latencies.
[00:45] Priya Shah: Also security, we have some EU data residency needs and SAML SSO plus SOC2 baseline, so curious about Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs.
[01:05] Maya Chen: Totally. Jordan and I will cover both the pricing levers and ops/security. Quick q: do you currently self-host any models or use a hosted API?
[01:20] Raj Patel: We're mainly on OpenAI for prototypes, plus some self-hosted Llama instances for internal tests. Cost is getting out of hand on OpenAI for production so evaluating options.
[01:38] Jordan Park: Got it, yeah common pattern. For economics we look at per-token on hosted, and Reserved/Dedicated is basically a different cost shape — you trade commit for lower unit cost. Example (ballpark): hosted generation might be around $0.03-$0.06 per 1k tokens for completion depending on model, whereas dedicated reserved capacity can bring effective token-equivalent costs down 30-60% depending on utilization and model. (note: numbers are illustrative and we will send exact sheets).
[02:10] Liam O'Connor: That range helps but can you explain where batching/caching fit? Our traffic is spiky and a lot of repeated prefixes.
[02:28] Jordan Park: Yes — two big levers: batching (server-side request batching) and prefix/KV caching. Batching amortizes per-request overhead across many tokens, improving throughput and lowering cost per token under sustained load. KV cache lets you avoid recomputing prefixes for repeated contexts — that can cut downstream token compute a lot for high-reuse flows.
[02:54] Priya Shah: Is that automatic or we have to code it in our app?
[03:05] Jordan Park: We provide runtime-level prefix caching and automatic batching in Redwood Dedicated and Hosted; on Private you can enable the same features but you'll manage infra. There are TTLs and cache invalidation semantics you control. For best results you'll combine client-side shaping (group similar requests) with server-side batching.
[03:32] Liam O'Connor: Any numbers on savings? Like percent reduction?
[03:40] Jordan Park: In customer cases with high prefix reuse we've seen 20-60% reduction in token compute. Batching impact depends on latency SLO — if you can accept 100-200ms extra, batching windows help a lot. If you need sub-50ms p95, less batching.
[03:58] Raj Patel: Our SLA target is p95 < 300ms for short responses, longer for completions. Is Dedicated necessary to hit that?
[04:12] Maya Chen: Not necessarily. Hosted can meet that if you pick low-latency regions and smaller models, but Dedicated gives you predictable throughput and isolation. Dedicated also lets you tune autoscale and burst policies; for consistent traffic and cost predictability it's often the right move.
[04:35] Priya Shah: How do reserved discounts work? Example commitment sizes?
[04:45] Maya Chen: We generally do monthly/annual reserved capacity contracts — discounts scale with committed GPU-hours or total throughput. Typical mid-market deals see 30-50% off hosted equivalent with a 12-month commit. We have flexible burst vouchers so you're not strictly limited.
[05:05] Liam O'Connor: When you say "hosted equivalent" is that normalized to tokens or to GPU usage?
[05:12] Jordan Park: We do both in the spreadsheet — show effective $/1k-token assuming your latency profile and model mix, and also show GPU-hour TCO for on-prem/private scenarios. It's important because models with longer context or more decoder compute skew token math.
[05:29] Priya Shah: We're also curious about quantization and model variants. If we quantize can we push cheaper hardware?
[05:38] Jordan Park: Yes, quantization profiles are a lever — Redwood's runtime supports int8/int4 paths that can run on cheaper GPU types and give good perf for many models. That reduces cost but may have quality tradeoffs; we recommend evaluation on your prompt set. Redwood Optimize also suggests profiles per workload.
[05:58] Liam O'Connor: Ok that ties into benchmarking — we'd want to run our prompts through a few configurations. What's the typical pilot?
[06:07] Maya Chen: Usually a 2-4 week pilot: you provide sample traces, we run benchmarks on Hosted and Dedicated equivalents, test batching/caching configurations, and report p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, and cost-per-1k projections. Jordan will draft the plan.
[06:25] Priya Shah: Security: what about KMS/HSM integration and audit logs for Private?
[06:33] Jordan Park: Private or Dedicated with private control plane supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations. Audit logs and RBAC are available across tiers; Private gives you full network control (VPC, air-gapped if needed). We'll attach the SOC2/infra docs.
[06:52] Raj Patel: Any gotchas on data retention with Hosted? We can't store EU PII off-region.
[06:58] Maya Chen: We support region pinning for Hosted and data controls; for strict residency Private is recommended. We'll detail options in the security doc.
[07:12] Speaker 1: (inaudible) question about how token counting works — you said prompt vs completion fees?
[07:20] Jordan Park: Right, typically billed on request tokens + response tokens; some customers model only completions for cost forecasting but we include both. We'll show sample bill calc for your workload.
[07:36] Liam O'Connor: For our numbers, assume 60% prompt, 40% completion token split, average response length 120 tokens. Does that change which tier is best?
[07:49] Maya Chen: It changes the math but not the levers — Dedicated helps more when you have sustained throughput and predictable patterns; Hosted is easier if you're early and want to avoid commit. We'll model both with your split.
[08:05] Priya Shah: On integration effort — how long to onboard Dedicated?
[08:12] Jordan Park: Typical Dedicated onboarding is 4-6 weeks with a basic config and integration; Private on-prem can be longer depending on infra. Hosted is immediate. We'll include a rollout plan.
[08:25] Liam O'Connor: What about failure modes — if Dedicated node fails do we auto-fail to Hosted?
[08:33] Maya Chen: We support cross-tier fallback policies — you can set an automatic fallback to Hosted or alternate region if Dedicated capacity is constrained. That's part of our graceful degradation story.
[08:48] Raj Patel: Can we run custom models in Dedicated? For example our fine-tuned model?
[08:55] Jordan Park: Yes, Dedicated supports customer-provided models; we help with model compatibility and kernel tuning. For Private you manage the model runtime though we'll provide guidelines.
[09:10] Priya Shah: For cost projection, can you show us an example 1M, 10M, 100M token month scenario?
[09:17] Maya Chen: We'll include that in the spreadsheet with assumptions for batching, cache hit rates, and model mix; that'll show per-token effective price across tiers.
[09:28] Liam O'Connor: Curious about cache hit modelling — if we get 40% cache hits what does that typically equate to in cost reduction?
[09:36] Jordan Park: If 40% of prefixes hit the KV cache, you could see effective compute drop roughly in that range — maybe 25-40% lower billable tokens depending on where hits occur. We'll recommend experiments to measure hit rates.
[09:50] Speaker 2: (mumble) Are there minimum commitments?
[09:55] Maya Chen: Minimums vary by tier and contract; Dedicated has commitments tied to reserved capacity; Hosted is pay-as-you-go. We'll detail ranges.
[10:05] Raj Patel: How elastic is Dedicated — will we be paying for idle GPU hours?
[10:12] Jordan Park: Reserved capacity expects some baseline utilization; we provide autoscale and burst credits so you don't overpay for low usage. The spreadsheet will show blended numbers.
[10:25] Priya Shah: Ok, can you walk through a sample pilot timeline?
[10:30] Jordan Park: Week 0: kickoff and traces; Week 1: baseline benchmarks on Hosted; Week 2: Dedicated config and caching tests; Week 3: perf tuning and quantization experiments; Week 4: report and next-step recommendation. Flexible based on your needs.
[10:50] Liam O'Connor: One more: how does model versioning and rollouts affect cost — if we roll multiple versions during A/B tests?
[11:00] Maya Chen: More variants increase total token consumption but also allow traffic splitting. Redwood Console shows per-model cost & latency breakdowns so you can quickly see regressions and rollback if needed.
[11:16] Raj Patel: Any references or customer examples for similar scale?
[11:21] Maya Chen: We can anonymize a few: a media customer cut token costs ~35% with Dedicated + prefix caching; a SaaS team used quantization to run models on cheaper GPU types and reduced infra spend by ~25%. We'll include case studies.
[11:40] Priya Shah: Sounds good. On security attachments — do you send a SOC2 report or a link to hosted docs?
[11:45] Maya Chen: We'll attach the cert PDF and a security FAQ link. For Private we'll include deployment checklist.
[11:55] Speaker 3: (brief crosstalk)
[12:00] Maya Chen: Ok, quick recap: we will send pricing spreadsheet, security docs, and Jordan will draft benchmark/pilot plan. Horizon will share traces and confirm internal stakeholders.
[12:15] Liam O'Connor: Great, let's do that.
[12:20] Priya Shah: Thanks all.
[12:25] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the materials and a calendar invite for the deep dive.

End of transcript. Note: transcription includes occasional mis-heard words and imperfect punctuation as recorded by Fireflies export.
